albums.blurb: Recorded live at New York's Village Vanguard on June 25, 1961, this set captures the trio of Bill Evans, bassist Scott LaFaro, and drummer Paul Motian — the group that reinvented the piano trio as a three-way conversation rather than a soloist with accompaniment. It was the trio's final recording: LaFaro died in a car accident eleven days later, and the album (with its companion Waltz for Debby, drawn from the same day's sessions) became the definitive document of a band that shaped nearly every piano trio since.
albums.reception: Routinely ranked among the greatest live jazz recordings ever made, the album was inducted into the Grammy Hall of Fame in 2010.

albums.blurb: Clairo's third album trades the hushed folk of Sling for warm, live-on-tape soft rock and soul, produced with Leon Michels of El Michels Affair and played by his Daptone-orbit crew, including drummer Homer Steinweiss and trumpeter Dave Guy. It is also her first self-released record, built on Wurlitzer, flute, and analog tape hiss rather than the bedroom-pop laptop textures she started out with.
albums.reception: Charm debuted at No. 8 on the Billboard 200 — Clairo's highest chart placement to date — and was nominated for Best Alternative Music Album at the 67th Grammy Awards.

albums.blurb: Ebo Taylor, born 1936 in Cape Coast, is one of the architects of modern Ghanaian music — a guitarist and arranger who studied in London alongside Fela Kuti in the early 1960s and spent the following decades folding jazz, soul, and Afrobeat into traditional highlife. Conflict, cut in 1980 with his band Uhuru Yenzu, is widely treated as the peak of that run: five long tracks of horn-driven Afro-funk, closing with 'Victory,' an arrangement of a traditional Asafo song.
albums.reception: Long a collector's item after its 1980 release, the album was returned to print by the Mr Bongo label in 2013 with a further vinyl reissue in 2021, and The Vinyl District's Graded on a Curve column singled it out for a full review.
